thumb_title: A photo is a tiny slice
thumb_sub: Say no and tell your grown up
hook: How to tell a five year old a photo is not the whole person

caps: Hello, I'm DiGi. This one is for you and your grown up.
So snuggle up. Ready?
Before we start, let's do our big breath.
Breathe in, and out.
One more.
In, and out.
Lovely.
This is our very first adventure together, and I promise you,
screens are better together.
Today we learn one big thing.
Things on a screen can look different from real life.
And if anything on a screen ever makes you feel funny inside,
you can say no and tell your grown up.
Say our special word. Tell.
Look at this photo. Big smile.
Lovely, isn't it?
But here's a little secret.
A photo only shows a teeny tiny slice.
The real you laughs out loud. The real you gives warm hugs.
The real you feels happy and sad and silly.
Sometimes all in one day.
A photo can't do any of that.
And here's the even bigger secret.
It's not just your photo.
Other people and other things on screens
can look different from real life too.
Someone might look super friendly in a video
and be different in real life.
A game might look like a lovely present and not be one.
Screens only ever show us a slice. Never the whole thing.
And you know what?
Things on screens can make us feel things too.
Some things make us giggle.
Some things make us feel warm and happy.
And sometimes something makes us feel funny or wobbly inside.
All of those feelings are okay. And all of them matter.
Pause me here, grown up. Ask your little one:
what can the real you do that a photo can't?
And if your child is six or seven, ask this too.
Can you think of a time something on a screen looked different from real life?
I'll wait.
Here's a lovely thing you might hear tonight.
A child might say, "Hey, that photo doesn't show me being funny."
And the grown up says, "You're right.
No photo can show all the wonderful you."
A screen shows a slice of you.
A mirror shows the real, whole you.
Alive and wiggly, right now.
And just like your photo isn't the whole you,
things on screens aren't always the whole story either.
So here is the most important bit of all.
If anything on a screen ever makes you feel funny or wobbly inside,
you can say no. You can put the screen down.
And you can tell your grown up.
Telling is always, always a good idea.
You will never be in trouble for telling.
Grown up, this one is yours to say.
Pause me and tell them,
"You can tell me about anything you see on a screen,
and how you feel always matters to me."
If your child is six or seven, ask them too:
what would you do if something on a screen made you feel funny inside?
Say it like you mean it, because you do.
Now our special sentence, three times. Big voices!
Real me is the whole me.
Real me is the whole me.
Real me is the whole me.
Tonight, play the mirror game.
Take one photo of your child, then stand together at a mirror.
Ask them, "What can the real you do that the photo can't?"
Then wiggle, giggle, and pull the silliest face in the world.
lines.say: Ask them, what can the real you do that the photo can't? Then wiggle, giggle, and pull the silliest face in the world.

caps: The photo stays still, but the real you can do anything.
Then play one more round.
Grown up, ask, "If something on a screen made you feel funny inside,
what would you do?"
And let your little one shout it out.
"Say no and tell my grown up."
Give them a great big cheer.
Before I go, show your grown up one thing you remember from today.
Anything at all.
Got it? Brilliant.
Remember, screens are better together.
See you next time.
